ch-foundations.text: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models1 Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value 1 Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value Nerve cells communicate with brief electrical spikes. This chapter explains how firing rates across a group of cells can represent an eye angle or an animal’s location, and how variable spike timing affects that representation. These ideas supply the biological and probability background for the three papers. The eyes can hold a position after a brief movement command has ended. An animal can also keep track of its location while the activity of individual neurons fluctuates. Both abilities require a useful quantity to remain represented in a changing biological system. The three papers study different parts of this problem: the loss of a stored value, the origin of slow eye motion, and the arrangement of spatial firing patterns. Before asking how a circuit keeps a value, we need to know how its activity represents that value and what makes the activity variable. We begin with the spikes that cells send and the patterns of firing rates across a population. A model of spike counts then shows why one brief observation can be uncertain and how combining counts from several cells can help. We then learn how to tell whether measurements vary together and how to separate random spreading from a change in the average value. Those distinctions will let us interpret both a memory model and measurements of eye motion. 1.1 Patterns of firing rates represent a value A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called spikes. A firing rate is the expected number of spikes per unit time. A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds. Neurons affect one another through connections called synapses. In the models used here, inputs have two contrasting effects: An excitatory input increases a receiving neuron’s tendency to fire. An inhibitory input reduces it. The effect of a spike can last beyond the spike itself because synaptic input decays over time. When neurons send signals back into the same population, the circuit has recurrent connectivity. Such feedback can maintain activity after an external signal disappears. A tuning curve gives a neuron’s expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable. For eye angle \(\theta\), a simple local model is \(r_i(\theta)=b_i+k_i\theta\). Neuron \(i\) has baseline rate \(b_i\) in spikes per second and slope \(k_i\) in spikes per second per degree. The linear expression can describe an active range, but it must be modified where it would predict negative firing. The eye paper includes a firing threshold and terms for movement as well as position.1 Different cells have different tuning curves. The vector \[ \mathbf r(\theta)=\bigl(r_1(\theta),\ldots,r_N(\theta)\bigr) \] is a population code: the pattern across \(N\) neurons carries information about \(\theta\). The position of a cell in this vector is a neuron identity, rather than a location in physical space. Reading a value from observed spikes is decoding. Establishing a population pattern from an input is encoding. The 2012 paper asks how accurately the network can maintain such a pattern using its own noisy activity. Spatial tuning gives a second example. In the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory and navigation, a place cell fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. A connected region of elevated spatial firing is a place field. One neuron can have several fields. A rate map estimates the rate at each position by dividing the spikes recorded there by the time spent there. Sparse visits, smoothing, and firing cutoffs therefore affect the estimated map and its fields. A field in a model’s expected rate and a field extracted from finite recordings are related objects with different measurement uncertainties.2 The hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1 contain place cells, but their connections differ: CA3 supplies major input to CA1 and has substantial recurrent excitation. CA1 also receives input from entorhinal cortex and has much less local recurrent excitation. A grid cell, found in entorhinal cortex, has repeated spatial fields that often form an approximately hexagonal pattern in a two-dimensional arena. These repeated grid fields and a place cell’s irregular multiple fields should be kept distinct. A model explaining CA1’s output maps need not identify where the animal’s position estimate is maintained.3 1.2 A variable spike count at a fixed rate A tuning curve describes expected activity, but a brief spike observation can differ each time the same value is represented. The 2012 model describes this variability with a Poisson process. At constant rate \(r\), the number \(K\) of spikes in an interval of length \(\Delta t\) obeys \[ \Pr(K=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}, \qquad \lambda=r\Delta t, \qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots . \] Here \(\lambda\) is an expected count, so it has no units. For this distribution, \[ \mathbb E[K]=\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=\lambda. \] Derivation: why a Poisson count has variance equal to its mean Summing \(k\Pr(K=k)\) gives \(\lambda\). Likewise, summing \(k(k-1)\Pr(K=k)\) gives \(\lambda^2\). Since \(K^2=K(K-1)+K\), \[ \mathbb E[K^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=\mathbb E[K^2]-\mathbb E[K]^2=\lambda. \] The count variance grows with rate, while its size relative to the mean falls. Its relative standard deviation is \(\sqrt\lambda/\lambda=1/\sqrt\lambda\). This is why collecting more independent spikes can improve a rate estimate. It also means that increasing a firing-rate scale does not keep absolute noise amplitude fixed. Comparisons between networks must specify which quantities are held constant.4 Example: an apparently silent cell and an informative population Suppose the expected rate is 20 spikes per second and an observation lasts 50 ms. The expected count is \(20\times0.05=1\). The probability of seeing no spike is \(e^{-1}=0.368\). A silent interval is therefore common even though the expected rate is positive. Now suppose 20 conditionally independent cells each have that rate. Their total count is Poisson with mean 20 and standard deviation \(\sqrt{20}=4.47\). The total rate estimate has a relative standard deviation of about 22.4%, compared with 100% for one cell. Population averaging helps because the independent count variances add while the mean signal adds directly. If a common varying input makes several cells’ firing rates rise and fall together, that shared variation will not disappear in the same way. The two count distributions can be compared on the same rate per cell scale. Figure 1.1: Analytic teaching construction for the chapter’s 20 Hz, 50 ms example. The count is Poisson with mean 1 for one cell and mean 20 for 20 conditionally independent cells. Both panels plot the rate per cell \(K/(N\Delta t)\), so both estimates have mean 20 Hz; their standard deviations are 20 Hz and 4.47 Hz. Each stem is a probability at one possible estimate, rather than a continuous density. Only estimates through 100 Hz are drawn. The independence condition concerns fixed modeled rates, not complete recurrent spike trains. Dividing the pooled rate estimate by 20 keeps the expected rate per cell fixed, while independent averaging reduces its relative spread. See Poisson count likelihood, SI Eq. S43, p. 9. For changing rates, the expected count is the integral \(\lambda=\int r(t)\,dt\). In a recurrent network, \(r(t)\) itself depends on past activity. The useful independence statement is therefore conditional: given the current modeled state, the elementary spike-generation noise is independent across cells in the basic 2012 model. Averaging over the evolving state can still produce correlations across time and across neurons. This qualification prevents treating a recurrent Poisson network as a collection of independent complete spike trains. Two other measurements describe different aspects of variability: The coefficient of variation, or CV, of interspike intervals, the times between successive spikes, is their standard deviation divided by their mean. A homogeneous Poisson process has exponential intervals and CV equal to one. More regular firing can have CV below one, as in the ocular motor neurons analyzed in 2022. The count variance divided by mean count is the Fano factor; its value also depends on the counting interval. CV and Fano factor cannot be substituted for one another without additional assumptions. 1.3 Mean squared displacement combines random spread with mean motion To identify where variability enters a pathway, the eye paper compares measurements that share some fluctuations and have other fluctuations of their own. For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), covariance measures how their centered values vary together: \[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)= \mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])]. \] It has units equal to the product of the units of \(X\) and \(Y\). Variance is the special case \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)\). Expanding a centered sum or difference gives \[ \operatorname{Var}(X\pm Y)= \operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y) \pm2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y). \] Independence makes the covariance zero when the relevant moments exist. Zero covariance alone does not imply independence in general. The correlation coefficient rescales covariance: \[ \rho_{XY}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)} {\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. \] It has no units and lies between \(-1\) and \(1\) for variables with nonzero variance. The magnitude of a correlation is not automatically the fraction of an output variance caused by a particular source. Establishing that interpretation requires a model of the signal, noise, and measurement gains. The eye-drift covariance calculation supplies that model for eye displacement. The quantity that changes between two times is a displacement \(\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)\), where \(\ell\) is a time lag. Its mean square splits into \[ \mathbb E[(\Delta x)^2]= \operatorname{Var}(\Delta x)+\mathbb E[\Delta x]^2. \] Thus a growing mean squared displacement can contain random spread, a systematic change in the mean, or both. ch-persistence.text: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models2 Stable representations can accumulate error 2 Stable representations can accumulate error A neural circuit can sustain its firing while the value represented by that firing changes. Using eye angle as an example, this chapter separates changes in the activity of the cells from changes in the stored value. That distinction explains how persistent activity can still accumulate memory error. The next distinction is between a value and the activity that represents it. Eye position is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. Another disturbance can leave a coherent activity pattern while changing the value. The geometry of these two changes will explain why a stable-looking circuit can still accumulate memory error.1 We first build a small example in which some disturbances fade while others leave a different stored angle. We then ask what happens when small lasting changes arrive repeatedly, deriving how their spread grows with time and how a fixed bias changes that prediction. The final distinction is between this changing value and an irregular spatial map that stays fixed. It explains why the memory, eye-motion, and place-field papers need different models even though all three concern variable neural signals. 2.1 Stable activity with a vulnerable stored value A circuit’s current activities are its state. A dynamical equation specifies how that state changes. A fixed point is a state where the deterministic rate of change is zero. It is stable in a direction if a small disturbance in that direction decays. Memory of a continuous quantity calls for a family of persistent states. A continuous attractor is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model. The family is an attractor manifold. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit. A line attractor has one represented coordinate; a ring can represent a periodic coordinate such as heading.2 Example: two disturbances to the same stored angle Consider a teaching model with two activities \(r_1,r_2\) in spikes per second. Let \(b=40\) spikes per second and let \(k=2\) spikes per second per degree. A stored angle \(\theta\) corresponds to \[ r_1=b+k\theta,\qquad r_2=b-k\theta. \] The fixed points lie on the line \(r_1+r_2=2b\). Restrict attention to angles where both rates remain positive. Define the deviation in their mean activity and the represented angle as \[ x=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}-b, \qquad \theta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{2k}. \] Suppose each activity changes according to \[ \dot r_1=-a x,\qquad \dot r_2=-a x, \] where \(a>0\) has units inverse seconds. Adding and subtracting these equations gives \[ \dot x=-a x,\qquad \dot\theta=0. \] The first equation has solution \(x(t)=x(0)e^{-at}\), so disturbances in the common activity decay. The second equation retains any angle set by the initial state. At \(\theta=5\) degrees, the rates are \((50,30)\). Compare two disturbances from this same state: A disturbance of \((+3,+3)\) changes the rates to \((53,33)\). It creates \(x=3\) but leaves the represented angle at 5 degrees. The restoring dynamics return to \((50,30)\). A disturbance of \((+3,-3)\) gives \((53,27)\), with \(x=0\) and angle \(26/(2\times2)=6.5\) degrees. This state lies on the fixed-point line, so there is no restoring response. In the second case, the circuit remains coherent while holding the wrong angle. The two changes occupy different directions in the activity plane. The solid arrow in the figure is the restoring motion produced by the model. The dashed arrow shows the imposed disturbance along the fixed-point line, rather than a deterministic restoring flow. Figure 2.1: A common activity disturbance returns to the initial angle, while an along-line disturbance persists as a changed angle. The solid arrow is deterministic recovery; the dashed arrow is an imposed disturbance. This is the guide’s two-activity construction, not experimental data. This construction illustrates the geometry; it is not a fit to eye-neuron recordings. In a larger network, the direction that survives depends on its connection weights and cannot always be found by an ordinary perpendicular projection. The network calculation derives the correct projection from the network’s linearized dynamics. 2.2 Independent steps with equal duration and variance give linear variance growth If persistent angular changes arrive repeatedly, their errors accumulate. Divide time into intervals of length \(\Delta t\). Let \(\xi_j\) be the change in the represented coordinate during interval \(j\). The calculation assumes: increments are independent; each increment has mean zero; each increment has variance \(2D\Delta t\), where \(D\) has units coordinate squared per time. After \(n\) intervals, \[ \theta_n-\theta_0=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\theta_n-\theta_0) =\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_j) =2Dn\Delta t. \] Writing \(t=n\Delta t\) gives linear variance growth \(2Dt\). To describe this limit with a continuous path, use Brownian motion \(W(t)\). It starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero, and satisfies \(\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s\) for \(t\geq s\). It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation. In this continuous diffusion approximation, \[ \theta(t)=\theta(0)+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \mathbb E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]=2Dt. \] The parameter \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient. It measures the rate of variance growth; a single trajectory need not move monotonically away from its starting value. The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is \(2Dt\). A root mean squared displacement is its square root, \(\sqrt{2Dt}\), and has the same units as the represented coordinate. In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of \(2dDt\) only when each of the \(d\) coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention. Example: why the noise grows slower than a fixed bias Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient \(D=0.02\) degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is \(0.014\) degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. These are teaching values, not a new estimate from either monkey. If there is also a constant bias velocity \(v=0.10\) degrees per second, then \[ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. \] The deterministic and random contributions are equal at \(t=2D/v^2=4\) seconds. Their equal contributions there are each \(0.16\) degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must therefore account for systematic drift separately. Sample paths show the irregular motion; exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias. Figure 2.2: Simulated Brownian teaching paths and analytic displacement scales for \(D=0.02\) degrees squared per second and \(v=0.10\) degrees per second. The upper paths have zero drift and start at zero; the dashed envelope is the exact root mean squared displacement, not a boundary on individual paths. Below, \(\sqrt{2Dt}\) and \(vt\) are equal at 4 s, when each is 0.40 degrees. Their squares are the separate contributions to the biased model’s MSD. The coordinate is unbounded, and these chosen values are not estimates from animal recordings. A single path can turn back toward zero even while the root mean squared displacement grows. A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7. Two times along a Brownian path are correlated even though its increments are independent. For \(0\leq s\leq t\), write \(W(t)=W(s)+[W(t)-W(s)]\). The bracketed increment is independent of \(W(s)\) and has mean zero, giving \[ \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t)) =\operatorname{Var}(W(s))=s, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t))=\min(s,t). \] The same argument gives covariance \(2D\min(s,t)\) for a diffusing coordinate started at a fixed value. This identity is the intermediate step needed to compute the error from averaging a memory that moves during readout. It also helps explain why smoothing a diffusive input is different from smoothing a stationary noise source. A finite range, a periodic coordinate, external feedback, or a position-dependent diffusion coefficient changes long-time behavior. For example, ordinary squared angular distance on a ring cannot keep growing linearly forever. The basic \(2Dt\) result is local or unbounded unless those conditions are treated separately. 2.3 A fixed spatial map differs from a value that wanders over time The memory and eye papers study fluctuations that accumulate as time passes. The place-field paper instead starts with a random function of physical position. Once drawn for a cell and an environment, that function is fixed while the animal moves through the map. Revisiting a place evaluates the same expected-rate function, although the actual spikes can still vary from visit to visit. These two kinds of randomness can occur together. A circuit may maintain a position estimate with time-dependent noise, while downstream cells respond to position through irregular but repeatable tuning curves. Observing irregular spatial maps does not tell us how fast the maintained position drifts. Conversely, finding diffusion of a stored value does not determine the shapes of individual place fields. The following chapters develop the dynamical calculation first, then the experiment that tests a possible consequence, and finally the spatial statistics.3 The three questions can now be placed beside the kind of variation each paper studies. ch-memory-dynamics.text: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models3 Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor 3 Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor Burak and Fiete model a group of interacting neurons that retains a continuous value after an input ends. This chapter follows spikes through their effects at synapses and back into firing, then derives how random spike timing displaces the stored value. A network can keep firing after a stimulus disappears and still lose the value that the stimulus supplied. The important question is whether the activity pattern stays in the right place, not just whether activity continues. Burak and Fiete study this distinction in a network whose stable activity patterns form a continuous set.1 To calculate the loss of accuracy, we first describe how spikes renew synaptic activity as it decays. We then follow a small disturbance through the circuit’s return toward a stable pattern and identify the change in stored value that remains. Adding these lasting random changes gives a local rate of spreading. When connections have equal weights in both directions, we can express that rate using the cells’ tuning curves and check its meaning in a two-cell example. The following chapter asks how this local prediction extends to longer delays. Paper and Supporting Information (SI) links open the cited PDF page, near the passage where the viewer supports it. Use the equation, figure, or paragraph label to find the passage; the PDFs have no numbered text lines. The memory coordinate is \(\theta\). Its initial value is \(\Theta\). A bar denotes a noise free steady state, so \(\bar r_i(\theta)\) is neuron \(i\)’s steady firing rate at memory value \(\theta\). The common synaptic time constant is \(\tau\). A one dimensional diffusion coefficient \(D\) has units of memory coordinate squared per time, with the convention \(\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]=2Dt\) when \(D\) is constant and boundaries do not matter. 3.1 Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity Neural mechanism. How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. Incoming activations determine new firing rates; the resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended. The model assumes fixed connection weights, constant biases, a common synaptic decay time, and independent Poisson spike counts conditional on the present rates. The connections are tuned to a continuous family of steady patterns. The Gaussian description below also assumes weak fluctuations in total input. Mathematical derivation. To combine discrete events with continuous decay, a count process records the events and a decay equation records how their effects fade. Here \(N_i(t)\) counts neuron \(i\)’s spikes up to time \(t\). The activation \(s_i\) tracks the decaying synaptic effect of those outgoing spikes on receiving cells. It rises by one at each spike and otherwise decays: \[ ds_i=-\frac{s_i}{\tau}\,dt+dN_i(t). \] Equivalently, if its spikes occur at times \(t_i^\alpha\), \[ s_i(t)=\sum_{t_i^\alpha<t}\exp[-(t-t_i^\alpha)/\tau] \] after initial transients. Here \(s_i\) is dimensionless in the convention that each spike adds one unit. For five illustrative spike times, the plot shows the events and the activation they leave behind. Figure 3.1: Each spike adds one activation unit, which then decays with a 50 ms time constant. Closely spaced spikes add to the activation left by earlier spikes. The five spike times are an illustrative input, and the activation is calculated exactly from the chapter equation. The activation retains a decaying contribution from earlier spikes, so a spike train and its activation trace are different objects. The rate \(r_i\) has units of spikes per second. The summed input and the firing rule are \[ g_i=\sum_j W_{ij}s_j+b_i, \qquad r_i=\phi(g_i). \] The fixed weights \(W_{ij}\) say how neuron \(j\) affects neuron \(i\), and \(b_i\) is a constant input. The neural transfer function \(\phi\) converts total input into a nonnegative firing rate. For example, increasing input might increase firing linearly over some input range, or exponentially. The paper allows general connectivity and transfer functions at first (Model, Eqs. 7–9, p. 5).2 Conditioned on the present rates, spike counts over a short interval \(dt\) are independent Poisson variables. Thus \[ E[dN_i\mid r_i]=r_i\,dt, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(dN_i,dN_j\mid\mathbf r) =\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. \] The symbol \(\delta_{ij}\) is one when \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Splitting the count into its mean and fluctuation gives \[ ds_i=\left[-\frac{s_i}{\tau}+\phi(g_i)\right]dt+dM_i, \qquad E[dM_i]=0, \quad E[dM_i dM_j]=\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. \] This is still a jump process. In the paper’s weak fluctuation approximation, many individually small spike contributions produce only small changes in each neuron’s total input. Their summed fluctuation can then be represented by Gaussian noise with the same leading mean and covariance: \[ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt{r_i}\,dB_i, \qquad F_i(\mathbf s)=-s_i/\tau+\phi\!\left(\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i\right), \] where the \(B_i\) are independent standard Brownian processes. The noise coefficient has units \(\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}\), so its product with \(dB_i\) is a dimensionless activation increment. The Gaussian approximation is for small fluctuations in total input. It does not require each single neuron’s entire spike train to look like a Gaussian process (SI Eqs. S2–S5, p. 2).3 The supplement makes this limit concrete by replacing each population with \(n\) equivalent neurons and dividing each connection weight by \(n\). A summed input has a mean proportional to \(n/n=1\), while its variance is proportional to \(n/n^2=1/n\). Increasing population size therefore keeps the mean dynamics fixed and reduces input fluctuations. For a ring network, a neuron’s preferred angle is an angle where its tuning curve peaks. Increasing the density of equally spaced preferred angles and scaling weights as \(1/N\) serves the same purpose. The paper’s formulas give the leading terms in this large population limit, rather than exact finite network identities.4 Setting noise to zero gives the deterministic rate dynamics \(\dot{\mathbf s}=\mathbf F(\mathbf s)\). A continuous attractor is a family of fixed points satisfying \[ 0=-\frac{\bar s_i(\theta)}{\tau} +\phi[\bar g_i(\theta)], \qquad \bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta). \] Interpretation. In the noise free dynamics, recurrent firing balances synaptic decay at each fixed point. The network must be tuned to possess this family. An arbitrary recurrent network will generally have isolated fixed points rather than a whole line or ring of them. 3.2 The network’s return flow determines the lasting memory change Neural mechanism. A spike perturbs many aspects of a network’s state. Most of those changes decay as the state returns to the attractor. To calculate memory loss, we need the one change that survives: the displacement to a different fixed point. We assume a smooth continuous family with one neutral memory direction, while all other local modes decay. The disturbance must be small enough that the first order response describes the return flow. Mathematical derivation. A linearization keeps the terms proportional to a small perturbation and drops terms quadratic or higher in it. Here the network activation is \(\mathbf s=\bar{\mathbf s}(\theta)+\delta\mathbf s\). Taylor expansion of the transfer function gives \[ \phi\!\left(\bar g_i+\sum_j W_{ij}\delta s_j\right) \simeq\phi(\bar g_i)+\phi'(\bar g_i)\sum_jW_{ij}\delta s_j. \] The constant terms cancel because \(\bar{\mathbf s}\) is a fixed point. Therefore \[ d\delta\mathbf s=K\delta\mathbf s\,dt+R^{1/2}d\mathbf B, \qquad K_{ij}=-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\tau}+\phi'(\bar g_i)W_{ij}, \qquad R=\operatorname{diag}(\bar r_i). \] In this leading local calculation the noise strengths are evaluated at the fixed point. The entries of \(K\) have units of inverse time.5 Moving a little along the fixed point family changes the activation by \[ \delta\mathbf s\simeq\mathbf u\,\delta\theta, \qquad u_i=\frac{d\bar s_i}{d\theta}=\tau\frac{d\bar r_i}{d\theta}. \] Differentiate the fixed point equation \(\mathbf F[\bar{\mathbf s}(\theta)]=0\). The chain rule gives \[ K\mathbf u=0. \] Thus \(\mathbf u\) is a right zero eigenvector: a state direction that the linear dynamics neither restores nor amplifies. It is the tangent to the attractor. The other modes must decay for this local family to be attracting. We also need a left zero eigenvector, a vector \(\mathbf v\) satisfying \[ \mathbf v^T K=0, \qquad \mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1. \] Its purpose is to extract the lasting memory displacement from a general perturbation. The normalization makes \(\mathbf v^T(\mathbf u\,\delta\theta)=\delta\theta\). If a stable mode \(\mathbf z\) satisfies \(K\mathbf z=\lambda\mathbf z\) with \(\lambda\ne0\), then \[ 0=\mathbf v^T K\mathbf z=\lambda\mathbf v^T\mathbf z, \] so \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf z=0\). The left vector discards every decaying mode (SI Eqs. S12–S13, p. 3). Consequently the surviving part of a small perturbation is \[ \delta\mathbf s_{\mathrm{surviving}} =\mathbf u\,(\mathbf v^T\delta\mathbf s). \] Interpretation. This generally differs from a perpendicular geometric projection. Decay can be tilted relative to the tangent. Even symmetric synaptic weights do not usually make \(K\) symmetric, because \(\phi'(\bar g_i)\) multiplies different rows by different amounts. Example: a disturbance that slides while it decays. To see the distinction without a neural simulation, consider the local system \[ \dot x=ay,\qquad \dot y=-\lambda y,\quad\lambda>0. \] Every point with \(y=0\) is fixed. Starting from \((x_0,y_0)\) gives \(y(t)=y_0e^{-\lambda t}\) and \[ x(\infty)=x_0+\frac{a}{\lambda}y_0. \] Here \(\mathbf u=(1,0)^T\) and \(\mathbf v=(1,a/\lambda)^T\). A vertical perturbation changes the final memory whenever \(a\ne0\). A perpendicular projection would miss that change. This is a teaching example of the projection geometry, not an additional network used in the paper. Figure 3.2: Original guide construction of the tilted decay example, with dimensionless coordinates and \(a/\lambda=1/2\). After an imposed jump from \((0,0)\) to \((0,2)\), the state relaxes toward \((1,0)\); successive time marks crowd toward that endpoint. This illustrates the left and right zero vector construction in Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, Section II, pp. 3–4, Eqs. S10–S16; it is not a paper network simulation. As y decays, x changes by one; the left vector extracts that lasting shift. 3.3 Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient Neural mechanism. We can now calculate how much random displacement remains after the stable components have relaxed. Each cell’s random spikes disturb its outgoing synaptic activation; the circuit’s return flow determines the lasting shift in memory. This calculation uses the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions, with rates and return flow evaluated near one fixed point. Mathematical derivation. The variance of a linear combination of independent noise increments is the sum of their variances multiplied by squared weights. Here the weights are the components of \(\mathbf v\): multiply the linear stochastic equation by \(\mathbf v^T\). Since \(\mathbf v^TK=0\), \[ d\theta=\mathbf v^T R^{1/2}d\mathbf B =\sum_i v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}\,dB_i. \] The independent Brownian increments have covariance \(E[dB_i dB_j]=\delta_{ij}dt\), so \[ E[(d\theta)^2] =\sum_{ij}v_iv_j\sqrt{\bar r_i\bar r_j}\,E[dB_i dB_j] =\left(\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\right)dt. \] Matching this to \(2D\,dt\) yields the general local result (SI Eqs. S14–S15, p. 3) \[ \boxed{2D(\theta)=\sum_i v_i(\theta)^2\bar r_i(\theta).} \] For several memory coordinates \(\theta_\alpha\), choose tangent vectors \(u_i^\alpha=\partial\bar s_i/\partial\theta_\alpha\) and left vectors with \(\sum_i v_i^\alpha u_i^\beta=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\). The same covariance calculation gives \[ 2D_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i v_i^\alpha\bar r_i v_i^\beta. \] Interpretation. For one memory coordinate, each neuron’s contribution combines its spike variability, \(\bar r_i\), with the squared effect of one activation fluctuation on the final memory, \(v_i^2\). The formula does not say that neurons with high rates necessarily damage memory more: changing rates can also change the tuning curves and the projection weights. Those changes must be included in a comparison.6 The result is local in state and leading order in weak noise. The time interval must satisfy two conditions: It must be long enough for the approximation based on many spike contributions to apply. It must be short enough that the coefficients do not change substantially as the memory moves. These conditions justify a local spreading rate. Systematic drift requires a separate check in the next chapter. The diffusion tensor is the matrix of displacement covariances per twice the elapsed time. Its diagonal entries describe spreading in individual coordinates; its other entries describe how coordinate displacements vary together. Even independently generated spike-count fluctuations can generate coupled motion of the represented coordinates.7 3.4 Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves Neural mechanism. The general formula requires the left vector of the network dynamics. When \(W_{ij}=W_{ji}\), can we express it through the tuning curves and neural transfer function? Symmetric connections make each cell affect another cell’s input with the same weight that it receives in return, while their firing responses can still differ. We retain the common synaptic time constant, a stable continuous family, and the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions. Mathematical derivation. The chain rule relates the slope of a response curve to the slope of its input curve. Here let \(g_i'=d\bar g_i/d\theta\) and \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\). Differentiating the fixed point identities gives \[ r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i', \qquad \mathbf g'=\tau W\mathbf r'. \] With symmetric \(W\), the transpose of the linearized matrix satisfies \[ K^T\mathbf g' =-\mathbf g'/\tau+W\operatorname{diag}[\phi'(\bar g_i)]\mathbf g' =-\mathbf g'/\tau+W\mathbf r'=0. \] Therefore \(\mathbf v\) is proportional to \(\mathbf g'\). Its normalization is \[ v_i=\frac{g_i'}{\tau\sum_jr_j'g_j'}, \] because \(u_i=\tau r_i'\). Substituting into the noise projection gives \[ \boxed{ 2D(\theta)= \frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {\tau^2[\sum_i r_i'g_i']^2}. } \] Interpretation. The input slopes \(g_i'\) now determine the projection weights, so the diffusion coefficient can be calculated from the tuning curves and transfer function. This follows from SI Eq. S18, p. 4, with \(\bar g_i=\phi^{-1}(\bar r_i)\) wherever the transfer function is invertible over the relevant range. The supplied Early Edition main Eq. 2, p. 2 appears to omit the square on \(g_i'\) in the numerator; the projection calculation and SI S18 give the squared expression shown here. This is an independent source check, not an author-confirmed correction. The result requires: symmetric weights; a stable continuous family; the noise assumptions already introduced. The result does not require translation symmetry, in which shifting an activity pattern along the represented coordinate leaves the network dynamics unchanged in form.8 Example: opposite firing changes with constant diffusion. Take two mutually inhibiting cells with \(W_{12}=W_{21}=-1\), zero self weights, equal biases \(b\), and \(\phi(g)=g/\tau\) over the positive input range. Its fixed points obey \[ \bar s_1=\frac{b+\theta}{2},\qquad \bar s_2=\frac{b-\theta}{2},\qquad |\theta|<b. \] The coordinate is \(\theta=s_1-s_2\). The sum \(s_1+s_2\) relaxes to \(b\), while the difference is neutral. Here \(\mathbf u=(1/2,-1/2)^T\), \(\mathbf v=(1,-1)^T\), and \[ 2D=\bar r_1+\bar r_2=b/\tau. \] Although the two firing rates change with the stored value, their summed spike variability is constant. Therefore this network has constant local diffusion throughout its valid range. Near an endpoint, a negative linear rate would be impossible; a physical implementation must alter the transfer rule, and the interior formula alone does not describe that boundary. This model underlies the mutual inhibition example in Fig. 2E–G, p. 3.9 The plot uses \(b=20\) activation units and \(\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\). Figure 3.3: For the chapter’s two mutually inhibiting cells, b = 20 activation units and tau = 0.1 s give opposite changes in the two rates. Their sum remains 200 spikes/s, so local D remains 100 coordinate units squared/s. Open endpoints mark the excluded boundaries; the linear interior model does not determine boundary behavior. These curves are calculated examples, not simulation data. The dashed rate sum in the upper plot stays fixed, so the lower plot has the same \(D\) at every interior value of \(\theta\). ch-memory-information.text: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models5 Spike information limits memory stability 5 Spike information limits memory stability A neuron receiving spikes from a memory circuit has access to information about the stored value. This chapter sets a bound on estimation error under the model’s assumptions and derives the constraint that spike information places on the circuit’s memory stability. A neuron that receives spikes from a memory circuit can use them to estimate the value stored by that circuit. Collecting more spikes helps distinguish nearby activity patterns, but during collection the pattern itself keeps moving. The same variability that limits readout also perturbs the recurrent network. Burak and Fiete connect these two effects by deriving a lower bound on memory diffusion from the information in the spikes.1 The useful quantity is how clearly a short spike sample distinguishes nearby memory values. Comparing that quantity with the random motion already derived gives a minimum rate of memory spreading. This is a limit for a particular network, so using it to compare different networks also requires keeping track of what changes and what stays fixed. More information can permit better stability without ensuring that a particular circuit achieves it. We retain the memory coordinate \(\theta\), initial value \(\Theta\), firing rate \(\bar r_i(\theta)\), synaptic time constant \(\tau\), and diffusion convention \(\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D\Delta t\). The network projection determines which activity changes remain as changes in the stored value. 5.1 Rate slopes and spike variability determine local information Neural mechanism. Suppose two nearby memory values produce almost identical rates. A short spike sample cannot reliably tell them apart. If a small change in memory instead produces a large rate change relative to spike variability, that sample is more useful. We need a quantity that measures this local distinction. In a short interval \(h\), let \(n_i\) be neuron \(i\)’s count. Treat the memory state as locally constant and use the conditionally independent Poisson approximation from the neural model. The calculation below uses positive rates. Mathematical derivation. A likelihood is the probability of observed data as a function of a proposed parameter value. For the neural model, \[ p(\mathbf n\mid\theta)=\prod_i \frac{[\bar r_i(\theta)h]^{n_i}e^{-\bar r_i(\theta)h}}{n_i!}. \] Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum. With \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\), \[ \ell(\theta)=\log p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =\sum_i\{n_i\log[\bar r_i(\theta)h]-\bar r_i(\theta)h-\log(n_i!)\}, \] \[ S(\theta)=\frac{d\ell}{d\theta} =\sum_i\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i}(n_i-\bar r_i h). \] The score \(S\) measures how the log likelihood changes when the proposed memory value changes. Its mean is zero because \(E[n_i]=\bar r_i h\). Its mean square is \[ E[S^2] =\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i^2}\operatorname{Var}(n_i) =h\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. \] The cross terms vanish by conditional independence, and Poisson variance supplies \(\operatorname{Var}(n_i)=\bar r_i h\). Fisher information is this expected squared score. The paper divides it by observation duration and calls the result the internal Fisher information rate: \[ \boxed{J(\theta)=\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}.} \] To understand why inverse information is an error scale, let \(\hat\theta(\mathbf n)\) be an estimator whose mean equals \(\theta\) locally. Such an estimator is unbiased. Differentiate \(E_\theta[\hat\theta]=\theta\) with respect to \(\theta\). Under the usual conditions allowing differentiation through the sum over data, \[ 1=\sum_{\mathbf n}\hat\theta(\mathbf n)\partial_\theta p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =E[\hat\theta S] =E[(\hat\theta-\theta)S]. \] The last equality uses \(E[S]=0\). Cauchy Schwarz now gives \[ 1\le E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]E[S^2], \qquad \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge\frac{1}{Jh}.} \] Interpretation. This is the Cramér Rao bound. It is a local bound for regular unbiased estimation. It does not guarantee that every finite spike sample admits an estimator attaining it. The paper works in a weak noise, informative sample regime where local likelihoods can be approximated as Gaussian and efficient estimation can approach the bound. A prior distribution represents knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the spikes. A strong prior, bias, boundaries, or globally ambiguous tuning changes the estimation problem.2 If the coordinate is an angle in radians, \(J\) has units \(\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). The information in a locally stationary interval of duration \(h\) is \(Jh\), not \(J\).3 A vanishing rate requires a suitable limit and regularity of the likelihood. Each cell contributes squared slope divided by its count variance per unit time. High rates with zero slope do not distinguish neighboring values, so they contribute no local information. A sharply changing rate can be informative even if it is smaller than another cell’s peak rate. The coordinate here describes the network’s present internal state. It need not be a currently visible external stimulus. Sensory Fisher information has the same Poisson formula only when the stimulus dependent tuning curves are the relevant rates. Two positive tuning curves with the same changing part isolate the effect of extra baseline firing. Figure 5.1: Analytic teaching curves \(r_A(\theta)=5+35e^{-\theta^2/(2w^2)}\) and \(r_B(\theta)=r_A(\theta)+20\), in spikes per second, with chosen width \(w=0.6\) rad. The rates have the same derivative. Their individual Poisson information contributions \((r_i^{\prime})^2/r_i\) vanish at the rate peak, where the slope is zero, and are positive on the flanks. Adding baseline firing raises the count noise without changing the slope, reducing local information. These are illustrative tuning curves, not recorded neurons or a demonstrated attractor network. The rate peak has zero local slope, so it contributes no local information at that point. Extra spikes from a constant baseline increase Poisson variability without making nearby values easier to distinguish. See Internal Fisher information, Eq. 3, p. 2. 5.2 Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion Neural mechanism. The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. The lower bound on diffusion follows directly by comparing the state sensitivity of the network with the spike information. Mathematical derivation. Cauchy Schwarz bounds a dot product by the product of the two vector lengths. Here the normalization of the memory projection fixes that dot product, while the two lengths measure diffusion and information. From the projection and diffusion calculation, \[ 2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i, \qquad u_i=\tau r_i', \qquad \sum_i v_i u_i=1. \] Define two vectors \(a_i=v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}\) and \(b_i=r_i'/\sqrt{\bar r_i}\). Their dot product is \[ \sum_i a_i b_i=\sum_i v_i r_i'=\frac{1}{\tau}. \] Their squared lengths are \(\sum_i a_i^2=2D\) and \(\sum_i b_i^2=J\). Cauchy Schwarz therefore gives \[ \left(\frac1\tau\right)^2 \le\left(\sum_i a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)=2DJ, \] or \[ \boxed{D\ge\frac{1}{2\tau^2J}.} \] Interpretation. This proof uses the general left vector formula, so symmetric weights are unnecessary. It is a shorter teaching reconstruction of the scalar proof in SI Section V. Its assumptions are those used to derive \(D\) and \(J\); it is not a general statement about all possible noisy memory systems.4 The units agree: \(\tau^2J\) has units of time per coordinate squared, so its reciprocal has the units of diffusion. Small internal information forces a large minimum diffusion coefficient. Large information allows small diffusion, but does not guarantee it. Neural mechanism. Reaching the bound requires the network’s retained response to each cell’s spike noise to match that cell’s information about memory. A cell that adds retained noise without helping distinguish nearby values prevents equality. Mathematical derivation. Equality requires the two vectors in the proof to be proportional: \[ v_i=c\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i} \quad\text{for every contributing cell}, \qquad c=\frac{1}{\tau J}. \] Cells with zero tuning slope cannot contribute extra projected noise if equality is to hold. In a symmetric network, \(v_i\) is proportional to \(g_i'\), and \(r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i'\). At each state, the participating cells therefore need a common value of \(\phi'(\bar g_i)/\phi(\bar g_i)\). A sufficient way to satisfy this at all states is to choose that ratio equal to the same constant \(k\) throughout the relevant input range. Solving \[ \frac{d}{dg}\log\phi(g)=k \] gives \(\phi(g)=A e^{kg}\). Interpretation. This exponential family attains equality for symmetric weights with Poisson noise, under the other model assumptions. It is a sufficient condition, rather than a general necessity: the common ratio may depend on the current memory state.5 Check: equality can also hold with a linear transfer rule The mutual-excitation example supplies a counterexample to the unrestricted converse. Set its bias \(b_0=0\) and use the linear rule \(\phi(g)=g/\tau\) on positive inputs. Its fixed states are \(s_1=s_2=\theta>0\), with \(\mathbf u=(1,1)^T\) and \(\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T\). Both rates are \(\theta/\tau\), and both rate derivatives are \(1/\tau\). Therefore \[ 2D=\frac{\theta}{2\tau},\qquad J=\frac{2}{\tau\theta},\qquad 2DJ=\frac{1}{\tau^2}. \] Equality holds throughout this family even though its transfer rule is linear. At each state both cells receive the same input, and the ratio \(\phi'/\phi=1/\theta\) changes between states. A converse that forces an exponential rule needs additional restrictions linking the participating input values across cells and states. Continuous variation of the represented value alone does not supply them. This qualification concerns the source’s claimed converse, while leaving the information–diffusion inequality intact. Example: the same diffusion with a looser information bound. In the two cell mutual inhibition model, use \(b=200\) activation units and \(\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\). The memory coordinate is an activation difference, not an angle. At \(\theta=0\) both rates are \(1000\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and their slopes are \(\pm5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) per activation unit. Thus \[ J=\frac{25}{1000}+\frac{25}{1000}=0.05, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}=1000. \] Here \(J\) has units of inverse activation unit squared per second, and \(D\) has activation unit squared per second. The bound is \(1/(2\tau^2J)=1000\), so equality holds at this balanced state. At \(\theta=100\), the rates become \(1500\) and \(500\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\), while their slopes stay \(\pm5\). Now \[ J=\frac{25}{1500}+\frac{25}{500}=\frac1{15}\simeq0.06667, \qquad \frac1{2\tau^2J}=750. \] The actual diffusion remains \(1000\). The inequality is strict because these two unequal rates no longer align the network’s projection weights with the information optimal weights. This also shows why equality at a special state does not force the transfer function to be exponential on its whole domain. A constant lower bound attained everywhere and an accidental equality at one state are different claims. Figure 5.2: Analytic teaching calculation for the chapter’s mutual inhibition example, with \(b=200\) activation units and \(\tau=0.1\) s. The coordinate \(\theta\) is an activation difference. For positive rates \(r_{1,2}=(b\pm\theta)/(2\tau)\), \(J=2000/(40000-\theta^2)\) while \(D=1000\) activation units squared per second. The lower bound \(1/(2\tau^2J)\) equals \(D\) at \(\theta=0\) and falls to 750 at \(\theta=100\). Higher local information permits a lower diffusion bound but leaves the actual diffusion unchanged in this model. The plotted range stays inside the positive-rate domain \(|\theta|<200\). The gap at \(\theta=100\) shows why a lower minimum allowed by the inequality is not a reduction in the network’s actual diffusion. See Diffusion bound, Eq. 4, p. 3. Neural mechanism. When a circuit stores several coordinates, a spike can shift more than one of them. Comparing each coordinate separately would miss combinations of shifts. The information and diffusion must therefore describe these shared directions. Mathematical derivation. For \(m\) memory coordinates the information is a matrix, \[ J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i \frac{\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\, \partial_{\theta_\beta}\bar r_i}{\bar r_i}. \] The matrix calculation assumes that every independent small coordinate change can be distinguished through a change in rates, so \(J\) is invertible. The matrix bound \(2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\) means that every linear combination of coordinate displacements obeys the corresponding variance lower bound. Here \(A\succeq B\) means \(\mathbf z^T(A-B)\mathbf z\ge0\) for every real vector \(\mathbf z\). To derive it, form \(N\times m\) matrices \(U_{i\alpha}=u_i^\alpha/\sqrt{\bar r_i}\) and \(V_{i\alpha}=v_i^\alpha\sqrt{\bar r_i}\). Then \[ U^TV=I,\qquad U^TU=\tau^2J,\qquad V^TV=2D. \] Check: the residual matrix proves the lower bound Set \(Q=V-U(U^TU)^{-1}\). Expanding \(Q^TQ\) and using \(U^TV=I\) gives \[ Q^TQ=V^TV-(U^TU)^{-1} =2D-\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\succeq0. \] Interpretation. The bound controls every combination of stored coordinates, including coupled directions that separate scalar bounds would miss. If \(J\) is singular, this ordinary inverse formula cannot be used.6 5.3 Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed Neural mechanism. The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed. Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. The comparisons below control how added neurons, altered firing rates, or slower synaptic decay affect the tuning curves and recurrent input. Mathematical derivation. Increasing \(N\) while retaining the same distribution of tuning curves and scaling weights as \(1/N\) keeps individual inputs and rates fixed. The sums in the symmetric formula scale as \(N\) in the numerator and \(N^2\) in the denominator. Consequently \(D\propto1/N\), while \(J\propto N\). This is a controlled density or population replication comparison, not a promise about adding arbitrary neurons. If all tuning rates are multiplied by a factor \(a\), their slopes are also multiplied by \(a\), so \(J\mapsto aJ\). For equality achieving exponential networks, \(D\mapsto D/a\) immediately follows. The same scaling follows from the symmetric diffusion formula when the change preserves \(g_i'\) up to a common scale and preserves the tuning geometry. For a general fixed nonlinear transfer rule, multiplying rates need not preserve those quantities or even the attractor. The paper’s rate comparison is made with the tuning shapes and appropriate network scaling held under control.7 Changing \(\tau\) while holding the rate tuning curves and their input relation fixed gives \(D\propto\tau^{-2}\) in the symmetric formula. Maintaining those curves requires retuning the network, because \(\bar s=\tau\bar r\). In contrast, holding activation curves and dimensionless weights fixed in the linear two cell example makes rates scale as \(1/\tau\), so \(D=b/(2\tau)\propto\tau^{-1}\). Interpretation. These two statements concern different controlled comparisons. A larger cellular time constant can improve memory stability while the exponent of its effect depends on what the experiment keeps fixed. Neural mechanism. The paper also links tuning width to memory persistence. The reason for its opposite predictions in one and three dimensions can be derived from the number of active cells and their slopes. This derivation is a teaching reconstruction of the tuning width argument cited in the main text, rather than a proof that every tuning family follows one power law.8 Assume preferred positions \(\mathbf c\) have uniform density \(\rho\) in a \(d\) dimensional stimulus or memory space. Away from boundaries, let identical tuning curves have fixed peak rate \(a\) and a common shape \(f\): \[ \bar r_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta) =a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w]. \] The width \(w\) is varied while \(a\), \(\rho\), and the shape \(f\) are fixed. Mathematical derivation. For one coordinate direction \(\alpha\), replace the population sum by an integral and substitute \(\mathbf z=(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w\): \[ J_{\alpha\alpha} \simeq\rho\int d^d c\, \frac{a^2w^{-2}(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{af} =\rho a w^{d-2} \int d^d z\,\frac{(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{f}. \] Two factors determine how information changes with tuning width: The volume element contributes \(w^d\) because broader fields recruit more neurons. The squared slope contributes \(w^{-2}\) because broader curves change more slowly. Each diagonal entry therefore scales as \(J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{d-2}\). Now restrict the tuning shape \(f\) to depend only on distance from its center. Uniformly distributing those centers makes every coordinate direction equivalent: off-diagonal information terms vanish, and all diagonal entries are equal. For an exponential network that attains the matrix bound, \(D_{\alpha\alpha}=1/(2\tau^2J_{\alpha\alpha})\propto w^{2-d}\). Interpretation. The resulting comparisons are: Narrower curves help in \(d=1\). Width has no leading effect in \(d=2\). Broader curves help in \(d=3\). These conclusions change under another resource constraint. Fixing the total population spike rate instead of peak rate makes \(a\propto w^{-d}\), giving \(J\propto w^{-2}\) in every dimension. Sparse coverage, a large baseline rate, finite boundaries, correlated noise, or a width too small for the population integral can also change the comparison. Attaining equality means the network reaches the diffusion lower bound for its information rate and synaptic time constant. Minimizing diffusion still requires deciding how much information the allowed architecture and firing budget can supply. If an external stimulus produces the same tuning curves as the network’s input free memory states, the sensory and internal Fisher information are equal. In a symmetric exponential network, maximizing this information then improves sensory estimation and minimizes memory diffusion together. This is why the paper suggests that one circuit could support both sensory estimation and memory storage. The mathematical compatibility does not establish where a particular animal stores a memory, and the equality of tuning curves must be checked rather than inferred from the shared formula.9 Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. ch-memory-readout.text: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models6 Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed 6 Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement. When a recall cue arrives, the stored value has already moved. Later spikes can help estimate the value present at that cue, but they cannot reveal the particular random displacements that occurred before it. Waiting for more spikes also allows the network to move further. The question is how much observation helps when the value being read keeps changing. Separating the error accumulated during storage from the error of reading the cue state makes that question precise. Equal weighting of later observations shows why simply waiting can become harmful. Allowing for the state’s motion then shows how observation can keep helping toward a limit, and how access to only some spikes changes the useful duration. The time constants and noise assumptions also need checking before the resulting limits can be compared with the paper’s final error claim. As before, the memory coordinate is \(\theta\), its initial value is \(\Theta\), and its displacement variance is \(2Dt\) for constant diffusion coefficient \(D\) without boundaries or systematic drift. The storage delay \(T\) ends at the recall cue; the observation interval \(L\) begins there. The spike information rate \(J\) measures how clearly nearby present states can be distinguished, and \(\tau\) is the basic model’s common synaptic time constant. 6.1 Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions Neural question and model. At time \(T\), a recall cue arrives. The observer now wants the original value \(\Theta\), but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage. Even perfect knowledge of the state \(\theta(T)\) cannot recover its particular earlier random displacements. To solve the readout problem, the supplement approximates the likelihood from each short bin of duration \(h\) as Gaussian. Let \(x=\theta(T)\) and index subsequent bins by \(k\). The equivalent observation model is \[ \theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\eta_k, \qquad y_k=\theta_k+\epsilon_k, \] \[ \operatorname{Var}(\eta_k)=2Dh, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_k)=\frac1{Jh}. \] The Gaussian increments and observation errors are independent in this approximation. The value \(y_k\) summarizes information about the state from that bin’s population spikes; it is not an additional directly measured physical coordinate. The continuous limit is a convenient mathematical description of the many spike, weak fluctuation regime. It does not assert that an arbitrarily short physical bin already contains enough spikes for a Gaussian fit. The derivations below are exact within this local Gaussian readout model.1 Mathematical derivation. For an unbounded coordinate with constant \(D\) and no drift, let \(x=\theta(T)\) and let \(\widehat x\) estimate that state from later spikes. Write the storage displacement as \(s=x-\Theta\) and the readout error as \(e=\widehat x-x\). The total recall error is their sum: \[ \widehat x-\Theta=s+e,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(s+e)=\operatorname{Var}(s)+\operatorname{Var}(e) +2\operatorname{Cov}(s,e). \] Assume the readout is locally unbiased at every possible \(x\) and the future noise is independent of the storage history. Conditional on that history, the readout error then has mean zero. Since \(s\) is fixed by the history, \(\mathbb E[se]=\mathbb E[s\,\mathbb E(e\mid\text{storage history})]=0\). Both errors have zero mean, so their covariance vanishes. In this readout model, translation invariance means that shifting the represented value does not change the statistics of the readout error. Its variance is therefore the same at every \(x\); denote it by \(V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)\). Using \(\operatorname{Var}(s)=2DT\) gives \[ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L)=2DT+V_{\mathrm{read}}(L). \] Interpretation. The two terms describe different sources of error: \(2DT\) comes from storage. \(V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)\) concerns estimation of \(\theta(T)\) from spikes after \(T\). The supplement derives this decomposition for a locally translation invariant diffusion and readout model; state dependence, boundaries, informative priors, or uncertain initial encoding require corresponding changes.2 A timeline separates the displacement accumulated before the cue from the error in estimating the cue state afterward. Figure 6.1: Original guide construction of storage and cue state readout, based on Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, p. 12, Eq. S57. The illustrated path is one possible construction, and the orange estimate concerns the state at the cue rather than the state at the end of observation. With the conditions shown, storage and readout variances add because their cross covariance is zero. Later spikes can improve the estimate of \(x=\theta(T)\); they do not reveal the particular storage displacements that separated \(x\) from \(\Theta\). 6.2 Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long Neural question and model. A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from \(x\). Mathematical derivation. Write \(\theta(T+t)=x+B_D(t)\), where \(B_D\) has Brownian covariance \[ E[B_D(t)B_D(s)]=2D\min(t,s). \] The covariance arises because the two values share increments up to the earlier time. Their later increments are independent. The continuous average is \[ \hat x_{\mathrm{naive}}=\frac1L\int_0^L y(t)dt. \] Count noise contributes \(1/(JL)\): \(n=L/h\) bins, each of variance \(1/(Jh)\), give average variance \([n/(Jh)]/n^2=1/(JL)\). The motion contribution is \[ \frac{2D}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds. \] Split the square into its two equal triangles. On the triangle \(0\le s\le t\le L\), the minimum is \(s\). Therefore \[ \int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds =2\int_0^L\!dt\int_0^t\!s\,ds =\int_0^L t^2dt=\frac{L^3}{3}. \] Combining the terms gives \[ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{naive}}(L)=\frac{2DL}{3}+\frac1{JL}.} \] The two contributions have opposite dependence on \(L\). Differentiating, \[ \frac{dV_{\mathrm{naive}}}{dL}=\frac{2D}{3}-\frac1{JL^2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt{\frac3{2DJ}}. \] At that duration the two error terms are equal, and \[ V_{\mathrm{naive}}^{\min} =\frac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}. \] Interpretation. Waiting longer eventually increases error, even with more spikes available. The problem is their equal weighting for a moving state.3 6.3 Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit Neural question and model. An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without confusing them with direct measurements of \(x\). Their value is limited by the motion separating them from \(x\). This is an ideal inference rule for an observer; the readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval. Mathematical derivation. The precision of a scalar Gaussian estimate is the reciprocal of its variance. Independent Gaussian measurements of one value add precisions. To verify this, multiply likelihoods proportional to \(\exp[-(x-a)^2/(2V_a)]\) and \(\exp[-(x-b)^2/(2V_b)]\): the coefficient of \(x^2/2\) becomes \(1/V_a+1/V_b\). Let \(P(L)\) be the precision about the state at the beginning of an interval of length \(L\), using all observations in that interval and no informative prior. Suppose we have already compressed the later part into a likelihood about the next bin’s state with variance \(1/P\). Bringing that likelihood one step backward adds transition variance \(q=2Dh\), since the next state equals the earlier state plus an independent Gaussian increment. Its precision about the earlier state is therefore \[ \frac{1}{1/P+q}=\frac{P}{1+2DhP}. \] The new earliest observation adds precision \(Jh\). Thus, up to bin endpoint conventions that disappear as \(h\to0\), \[ P(L+h)=Jh+\frac{P(L)}{1+2DhP(L)}. \] Expand the denominator for small \(h\): \[ P(L+h)=P(L)+[J-2DP(L)^2]h+O(h^2). \] The continuous equation and starting condition are \[ \frac{dP}{dL}=J-2DP^2, \qquad P(0)=0. \] The hyperbolic tangent is \(\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})\). Its inverse hyperbolic tangent on \((-1,1)\) is \(\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]\), whose derivative is \(1/(1-z^2)\). Initially no observation means zero precision. The term \(J\) adds new information; the term \(2DP^2\) accounts for uncertainty when carrying that information backward through diffusion. Set \(a=\sqrt{J/(2D)}\) and \(k=\sqrt{2DJ}\). Separating variables gives \[ \int_0^{P/a}\frac{dz}{1-z^2}=kL, \qquad \operatorname{artanh}(P/a)=kL. \] Taking the inverse function and then the reciprocal yields \[ P(L)=\sqrt{\frac{J}{2D}}\tanh(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L), \] \[ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L) =\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L).} \] The hyperbolic cotangent is \(\coth z=1/\tanh z\). This backward precision derivation is a teaching reconstruction equivalent to the Gaussian covariance calculation in SI Eqs. S58–S75. It makes explicit how diffusion limits the value of later observations.4 For short intervals, \(\coth z=1/z+z/3+O(z^3)\), so \[ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)=\frac1{JL}+\frac{2DL}{3}+O(L^3). \] The naive and ideal estimators therefore agree through the displayed terms. For long intervals, \[ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)\longrightarrow\sqrt{2D/J}, \qquad L^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2DJ}}. \] Interpretation. The ideal observer keeps improving, but the improvement becomes small. Its variance relative to the limiting variance is: \(1.313\) at \(L=L^*\). \(1.037\) at \(2L^*\). \(1.005\) at \(3L^*\). These are variances, so their ratios are not ratios of standard deviations. Using \(2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}\) gives \[ L^*\le\tau, \qquad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt3L^*\le\sqrt3\tau. \] Thus the paper’s statement about readout within a cellular time constant concerns a characteristic saturation time under full spike access. It does not mean all benefit ends abruptly at \(\tau\). The naive observer’s best variance is only \(2/\sqrt3\simeq1.155\) times the ideal observer’s asymptotic variance. Its best standard deviation is about \(1.075\) times as large.5 6.4 Limited access can make observation slower Neural mechanism. A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network’s spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network. Mathematical derivation. If every spike is independently retained with probability \(\alpha\), the observed rates and their slopes both scale by \(\alpha\). Substitution in the Poisson information formula gives \[ J_{\mathrm{obs}}=\sum_i\frac{(\alpha r_i')^2}{\alpha\bar r_i}=\alpha J. \] The network diffusion coefficient stays \(D\). Hence \[ L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2D\alpha J}} =\frac{L^*}{\sqrt\alpha}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{ideal,obs}}(\infty)=\sqrt{\frac{2D}{\alpha J}}. \] Interpretation. The same factor \(1/\sqrt\alpha\) multiplies the naive optimal interval and its minimum variance. The information bound implies \(L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*\le\tau/\sqrt\alpha\), which can exceed \(\tau\). A selected subset of neurons has exactly \(\alpha J\) only when it carries that fraction of the information; a fraction of neurons or spikes chosen by a biased rule need not do so.6 Example: limited spike access changes the useful interval. Take \(\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\), \(J=10{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\), and \(D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}\). These values attain the information bound. Full access gives \(L^*=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\) and limiting readout variance \(0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). The naive optimum is \(0.1732\,\mathrm{s}\) with variance \(0.001155\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). If \(\alpha=0.1\), then \(J_{\mathrm{obs}}=1000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). The ideal characteristic interval becomes \(0.3162\,\mathrm{s}\) and its limiting variance becomes \(0.003162\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). The naive optimum becomes \(0.5477\,\mathrm{s}\). A two second storage delay contributes \(2DT=0.020\,\mathrm{rad}^2\) in both cases, giving total ideal asymptotic variances \(0.021\) and \(0.023162\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). Longer observation can reduce the readout cost; it cannot undo the random displacement during the delay. 6.5 Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition Neural mechanism. The time constant in the inequality comes from the dynamics that carry an activation fluctuation into a lasting memory change. If both synaptic activation and firing rate adjust gradually, which time constant matters? In the basic model, the firing rate changes immediately when the summed input changes. Assume symmetric weights. The extension instead lets \(r_i\) approach \(\phi(g_i)\) gradually, with time constant \(\tau_m\), while synaptic activation still decays with time constant \(\tau\): \[ \dot s_i=-s_i/\tau+r_i+\xi_i, \qquad \tau_m\dot r_i=-r_i+\phi(g_i). \] Here \(\xi_i\) is the zero mean noise from variable spike generation, with the same Poisson strength as in the basic model. Mathematical derivation. In this symmetric weight extension, the linear state is \((\delta\mathbf s,\delta\mathbf r)\) and its deterministic matrix is \[ A=\begin{pmatrix} -I/\tau&I\\ \operatorname{diag}(\phi')W/\tau_m&-I/\tau_m \end{pmatrix}. \] The right tangent is \((\tau\mathbf r',\mathbf r')\). Write the left zero vector as \((\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\). The second block of \((\mathbf a^T,\mathbf b^T)A=0\) gives \(\mathbf b=\tau_m\mathbf a\). The first then gives \(W^T\operatorname{diag}(\phi')\mathbf a=\mathbf a/\tau\), so symmetry again permits \(\mathbf a\propto\mathbf g'\). Normalizing its dot product with the right tangent yields \[ a_i=\frac{g_i'}{(\tau+\tau_m)\sum_jg_j'r_j'}. \] Only the \(s\) block receives the modeled spike noise, so \(2D=\sum_i a_i^2\bar r_i\). The symmetric formula consequently becomes \[ 2D=\frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {(\tau+\tau_m)^2[\sum_i g_i'r_i']^2}, \qquad 2D\ge\frac{J^{-1}}{(\tau+\tau_m)^2}. \] Interpretation. The sum of the two time constants replaces \(\tau\). The larger one dominates when they are very different. This result belongs to the two stage model and noise placement just described; the paper does not prove that arbitrary collections of biological time constants can always be added.7 Neural question and model. The equality condition also depends on the noise law. To see why, replace Poisson spike-count fluctuations with independent additive Gaussian noise of constant strength \(q>0\): \[ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt q\,dB_i. \] Mathematical derivation. The short interval observation of the mean rate is now Gaussian with variance \(q/h\). Repeating the score calculation gives \(J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/q\), while projection gives \(2D=q\sum_i v_i^2\). The same Cauchy Schwarz proof yields \(2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}\). Equality requires \(v_i\propto r_i'\) because all cells have the same noise strength. In a symmetric network \(v_i\propto g_i'\), so a linear transfer rule supplies the condition by keeping \(\phi'(g)\) constant across participating inputs. Interpretation. In the Poisson case, variance grows with rate and an exponential rule is a sufficient way to attain equality. The pointwise projection condition remains the general criterion, including the linear-family counterexample already derived. The difference between these sufficient classes follows from the noise weighting, not from linearity being universally preferable.8 This explicit \(q\) formulation is a teaching reconstruction that keeps dimensions and the noise normalization visible. The supplement’s Gaussian subsection establishes the change in equality condition. Here the matched noise and likelihood derivation supplies all factors of \(q\) and \(\tau\) without requiring the reader to infer a normalization from SI Eqs. S94–S95. 6.6 Readout saturates, and one printed error bound needs qualification Figure 3 isolates readout uncertainty, rescaling variance by \(\sqrt{2D/J}\) and duration by \(L^*\). In these axes the ideal curve is \(\coth z\) and the naive curve is \(z/3+1/z\). Both diverge like \(1/z\) at short durations because too few spikes are available. The plotted features are: The ideal solid curve approaches one. The naive dashed curve reaches \(2/\sqrt3\) at \(z=\sqrt3\), then rises because its equal weighting gives increasing importance to displaced states. The dotted vertical line marks that naive optimum. The storage delay contribution \(2DT\) is not part of these rescaled curves. Figure S2 repeats the comparison for partial access, showing the rightward and upward shifts when \(\alpha=0.1\).9 Figure 6.2: Original guide construction from the analytic readout formulas in Burak and Fiete (2012), Fig. 3 and Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S79–S81, rather than digitized data. Ideal readout approaches a normalized variance of one; simple averaging reaches \(2/\sqrt3\) at \(z=\sqrt3\) and then worsens. These curves contain no storage variance \(2DT\). More observation keeps helping the ideal reader, with diminishing benefit, while equal weighting eventually gives too much influence to a state that has moved. One printed inequality deserves special care. Main Eq. 6 says that total error is at least \(2D(T+\tau)\); SI Eq. S83 likewise uses a lower bound with readout term \(2D\tau/\sqrt\alpha\). But the paper’s other derived results imply \[ 2DJ\ge\tau^{-2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J\ge\frac1{2D\tau^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\le2D\tau. \] Thus the ideal asymptotic readout term is at most \(2D\tau\), with equality when the information diffusion inequality is saturated. Substituting an upper bound for this term cannot establish the printed universal lower bound on total error. Within the local Gaussian model, the defensible statement is \[ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L) \ge2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}, \] with equality approached as \(L\to\infty\) for the ideal observer. At saturation this asymptotic expression becomes \(2D(T+\tau)\). For partial access the same issue occurs with the factor \(1/\sqrt\alpha\). This is an apparent inconsistency between printed formulas, identified by algebra using the supplied sources. It is not a claim that the authors issued a correction.10 For a concrete strict inequality case, keep \(\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\) and \(D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}\) but set \(J=40{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Then \(2DJ=400\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\) exceeds \(\tau^{-2}=100\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\). The limiting readout variance is \(0.0005\,\mathrm{rad}^2\), whereas \(2D\tau=0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). At \(T=2\,\mathrm{s}\), the Gaussian ideal total limit is \(0.0205\,\mathrm{rad}^2\), below \(2D(T+\tau)=0.021\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). These values expose the algebraic problem without assuming the bound is saturated. When a continuous attractor circuit is used to accumulate an incoming signal over time, its stored value represents the integral of that signal. The short useful readout interval does not imply a short lifetime for this accumulated value. A tuned circuit can continue to represent the mean of accumulated inputs while its variance grows. A leak would instead pull its mean toward a particular value. Diffusion limits the accuracy of the integral and the usefulness of long observation; it does not by itself introduce that restoring pull. Applying these predictions to an animal also requires checking its spike statistics, tuning, drift, access to spikes, and other sources of movement noise.11 Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012).
