ch-eye-drift.text: Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code7 Eye drift points to a shared neural drive 7 Eye drift points to a shared neural drive Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism. Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called microsaccades, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.1 This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye’s movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions. 7.1 From stored eye position to muscle action The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The oculomotor integrator is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the foundations and network model stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.2 The signal reaches ocular motoneurons (OMNs), neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles. The recordings came from the abducens nucleus, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward. Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types using their eye movement response parameters. Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the ocular plant, turn neural activity into movement.3 There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. Private spike variability in individual OMNs. Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging. This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. 7.2 The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye’s angle while an electrode recorded one neuron’s spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement; there were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.45 The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals; they do not create 57 independent animal samples.6 The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell’s activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other. The diagram separates the physical pathway from the paired recordings and the later calculation of predicted eye position. Figure 7.1: The recordings pair one motor neuron with eye movement. Private spike variability acts at individual cells, downstream physical variability acts on movement, and measurement noise enters the eye-position record. The attractor storage source is proposed; the dashed analysis path is a calculation from one cell through its calibrated filter. Original guide schematic based on Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figs. 1–2 and 4–5. Signal symbols are illustrative, not experimental traces. The upper path describes a possible physical source and its output. The recording design provides one cell and eye movement at a time; it does not measure covariance between simultaneously recorded motor neurons. The predicted position is a later analysis result, not a signal sent backward through the physical pathway. 7.3 A fitted model links movement to firing rate Position alone does not predict a motor neuron’s activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits \[ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). \] Here \(E\) is horizontal eye position in degrees and \(\widehat f\) is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold \(E_T\) sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units \[ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. \] Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms. The delay \(\Delta t\) is in seconds: firing at time \(t\) predicts movement at the later time \(t+\Delta t\) for a positive neural lead. This is the paper’s Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.7 The observed rate \(f(t)\) was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. For each cell, the authors minimized the sum of squared rate errors, \[ L=\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\rm trials}}\sum_{t_j\in[0,T_a]} \left[f_a(t_j)-\widehat f_a(t_j;k,r,m,\Delta t,E_T)\right]^2. \] \(a\) labels trials and \(T_a\) is trial duration. This is Eq. 3 with the trial count renamed so that it cannot be confused with a neuron count. Fits used full trials, including fixation and pursuit. To predict a trial’s rate, that trial was left out of the parameter fit. Acceleration was estimated from velocity after local polynomial smoothing over 21 ms. Trials in which the rate fell below 20 Hz were discarded: the linear formula is intended for active cells above firing threshold, whereas firing cannot become negative.8 During fixation, the authors subtracted each segment’s mean firing rate, joined the segments, and compared observed and predicted rate fluctuations. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell; Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The one sided test asks whether the mean correlation is positive, compared with a zero-mean reference. Its p value is the probability, under that reference, of a test statistic at least as large as observed. Across 57 cells it gave \(p=3\times10^{-9}\). A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is the first evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.9 7.4 A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell’s spikes To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell’s spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals. Let \(x(t)=E(t)-E_T\). Ignoring the time shift for a moment, the deterministic relation is \[ m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f. \] A causal filter computes its present output from present and past input. For the equation above, its impulse response \(h_0(u)\) is the position response to one instantaneous spike at time zero. To factor the equation, consider a time component \(e^{pt}\): differentiation multiplies it by \(p\). The algebraic ratio of output to input for that component is \[ H_0(p)=\frac{1}{mp^2+rp+k} =\frac{1}{m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)}. \] Factoring the quadratic gives the slow and fast decay times \[ \tau_+=\frac{2}{r/m-\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}},\qquad \tau_-=\frac{2}{r/m+\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}}. \] These are the paired signs in the paper’s Eq. 7, with \(\tau_+>\tau_-\) when \(k,r,m>0\) and \(r^2>4km\). In this case both components decay without oscillation. The same factorization gives two useful identities: \[ \tau_+\tau_-=\frac{m}{k},\qquad \tau_++\tau_-=\frac{r}{k}. \] The corresponding impulse response is \[ h_0(u)=\frac{\Theta(u)}{m}\, \frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{\tau_+-\tau_-} \left(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}\right). \] \(\Theta(u)\) is zero for \(u<0\) and one for \(u>0\); it imposes causality. Restoring the fitted neural lead delays this response: \(h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)\). Write the spike train as \(\xi(t)=\sum_j\delta(t-t_j)\), where \(\delta\) is an ideal instantaneous impulse of unit area, so integration over one spike counts one event. The prediction is \[ \widehat E(t)=E_T+\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(t-v)\xi(v)\,dv =E_T+\sum_j h(t-t_j). \] These expressions reproduce Eqs. 4–6, including the factor \(\tau_+\tau_-/m\) and the delay. The convolution integral adds the responses to all past spikes. With spike count treated as a count, \(\xi\) has units spikes/s and \(h\) has units degrees/spike. Each spike contributes a decaying position response; adding those responses produces degrees.10 Derivation: the weights of the two decaying responses We can obtain the response to a spike directly from the differential equation. After the spike, the input is zero, and each of the two exponentials solves the remaining homogeneous equation. Write their combination as \[ h_0(u)=A e^{-u/\tau_+}+B e^{-u/\tau_-},\qquad u>0. \] To find \(A\) and \(B\), treat the spike as a short pulse of unit area and shrink its duration to zero. The position change during that pulse tends to zero, so \(h_0(0^+)=0\). Integrating \(m h_0''+r h_0'+k h_0\) across the pulse gives \(m h_0'(0^+)=1\): the velocity changes by \(1/m\), while position and velocity before the causal response are zero. Therefore \[ A+B=0,\qquad -\frac{A}{\tau_+}-\frac{B}{\tau_-}=\frac1m. \] Substituting \(B=-A\) gives \(A(1/\tau_- -1/\tau_+)=1/m\), hence \(A=\tau_+\tau_-/[m(\tau_+-\tau_-)]\). Making the response zero before the spike gives the impulse response \(h_0(u)\). For a constructed example, take \(k=4\) spikes/(s deg), \(\tau_+=0.120\) s, and \(\tau_-=0.005\) s. The identities above require \(r=0.500\) spikes/deg and \(m=0.00240\) spikes s/deg. Then \[ h_0(u)=2.174\left(e^{-u/0.120}-e^{-u/0.005}\right) \ \text{deg/spike},\quad u>0, \] and its area is \(2.174(0.120-0.005)=0.250\) deg s/spike, equal to \(1/k\). A steady rate of 80 spikes/s predicts an offset of 20 degrees above \(E_T\). This checks the gain as well as the time constants; it is not a fit to a recorded cell. Check: static gain and equal decay times The kernel’s area checks its normalization: \[ \int_0^\infty h_0(u)\,du =\frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{m(\tau_+-\tau_-)}(\tau_+-\tau_-) =\frac1k. \] Thus a constant input rate \(f_0\) predicts \(E_T+f_0/k\), exactly the static forward relation. A kernel with unit area would give the wrong conversion unless \(k\) had already been absorbed into the input. When the two decay times coincide, \(r^2=4km\), the limit is \(h_0(u)=\Theta(u)u e^{-u/\tau}/m\). The distinct exponential formula is used for the fitted responses in the paper. Figure 2a–b shows typical fitted times of about 5 ms and 120 ms. Figure 2c shows that a single cell’s reconstructed drift is much noisier than the measured movement. Across 350 ms displacement pairs, the mean Pearson correlation was \(\langle R\rangle=0.17\pm0.02\), where the error is the standard error of the mean (SEM). SEM estimates uncertainty in the across-cell mean, rather than the spread of individual cells or uncertainty across animals. The one sided test gave \(p=3.8\times10^{-12}\). Shuffling which measured segment was paired with which spike prediction centered the comparison near zero. Here and below \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) over cells means a population average.11 7.5 The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations? For a centered displacement \(Y\) and one centered prediction \(X\), the best linear prediction \(bX\) minimizes \(\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)\). Differentiating with respect to \(b\) gives \(b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)\). Its explained fraction of variance is \[ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. \] This is the coefficient of determination for a linear prediction with a fitted gain. It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error. Suppose there are \(N_m\) independent single neuron predictors \(X_i\). Standardize each to variance one and also standardize \(Y\). Independence makes the \(X_i\) uncorrelated, so the residual after using them all has variance \[ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y-\sum_i R_iX_i\right) =1-2\sum_iR_i^2+\sum_iR_i^2 =1-\sum_iR_i^2\ge0. \] Consequently \(\sum_iR_i^2\le1\), and an average neuron explains at most \(1/N_m\). This proves the bound used in Supplementary Eq. S1. It does not require equal muscle effects from all neurons. Applying it to the sampled cells does require their average explanatory power to represent the relevant motor population.12 The authors avoid directly averaging noisy squared correlations. Instead, \[ \langle R^2\rangle-\langle R\rangle^2=\operatorname{Var}(R)\ge0, \qquad \langle R^2\rangle\ge(0.17)^2=0.0289. \] Thus the estimated mean correlation implies an average explained fraction of at least about 2.9%. For 1,000 independently contributing motor neurons, the bound would be 0.1%; for several thousand it is smaller. The mismatch argues against independent OMN noise as the sole source. Shared fluctuations can allow many cells to explain the same part of the movement, so their explained fractions can overlap.13 This step finds shared variation. Locating its source upstream also uses a biological premise: the private variability generated within OMNs is taken to be independent across cells. The paper supports that premise using anatomical and stimulation studies indicating little local recurrent coupling in the relevant motor nuclei. It was not tested by simultaneous recordings in this data set. Common inputs can correlate the total activity of OMNs even when their privately generated spike noise is independent.14 7.6 Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the fact that the inverse filter has a calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as \[ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, \] where \(C=\delta E_C\) is the common upstream contribution, \(\eta\) combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and \(\epsilon\) is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes: The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale. \(C,\eta,\epsilon\) are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter: \[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). \] The common fraction is therefore estimated by \[ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. \] These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between \(\epsilon\) and \(\eta\), because the recorded neuron’s private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order \(1/N_m\) under its many neuron model.15 Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: \[ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. \] Large private noise in a cell inflates \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) and makes \(R\) small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there. Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82. These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with \[ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. \] Then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820\), all in deg\(^2\). It follows that \[ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. \] One cell explains \(R^2\simeq2.89\%\) of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise. Figure 7.2: The same common variance enters movement and the single cell predictor, but the predictor has much more private noise. Increasing only private predictor variance lowers correlation R while the common movement fraction χ stays at 0.82. The marked point uses the chapter’s constructed example. Calculations assume unit common gain and mutually uncorrelated contributions; they are not recorded cell data. Based on Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main p. 10, Eqs. 11–15. Private prediction noise enlarges the denominator of R without changing the covariance. The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10. In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate \(\chi_i\), and those estimates can lie outside \([0,1]\). The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error \(\Delta\chi_i\) mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: \[ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. \] To see the weighting, let normalized weights \(a_i\) sum to one. Independent errors give variance \(\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2\) for \(\sum_i a_i\chi_i\). Minimizing this subject to \(\sum_i a_i=1\) gives \(a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2\) and the error above. The paper additionally assumes approximately normal errors around a common value. The last expression is a propagated estimation error under those assumptions. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. The reported result was \(0.82\pm0.07\), a weighted mean and weighted error for horizontal displacement over 350 ms. It is neither a fraction of distance traveled nor the fraction that one neuron’s spikes accurately predict.16 Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). ch-synthesis.text: Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code13 Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests 13 Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests The three papers address different links between nerve-cell activity and behavior: retaining a value, producing eye movement, and representing location. This chapter compares what the models and recordings establish, and separates supported connections from further questions about how a complete neural circuit would work. A model can explain the shape of a neural code without explaining how that code is maintained. It can also explain fluctuations inside a circuit without uniquely locating the source of a measured behavior. Comparing the three papers requires keeping each claim with the mathematical or experimental test that supports it. To connect them, we first separate the spatial map, the changing represented position, and the movement measured downstream. A short calculation then shows how a common position error can make cells with different tuning change together. Comparing that calculation with each paper’s evidence and related studies identifies what a joint experiment would still need to measure. 13.1 The three papers constrain maps, dynamics, and movement For a circuit representing position, three questions arise: Spatial map: What activity pattern corresponds to each position? The place-field model addresses this question. Memory motion: How does the represented position evolve when there is no corrective input? The persistent-activity model addresses this question. Observed movement: How does a downstream physical system transform that changing signal into an observable movement? The eye-drift model combines a candidate account of memory motion with a detailed account of this transformation.1 The objects differ even when the word position appears in all three. In 2012, \(\theta(t)\) locates a network state on its attractor. In 2022, the internal eye-position command and actual eye angle are separate quantities linked through motor neurons and mechanics. In 2025, \(x\) locates an animal in an environment, and \(h_i(x)\) is a spatial input function assigned to a cell. The Gaussian process does not update a remembered \(x\) through time. The guide map gives a visual comparison of these three questions. Table 13.1: Comparison of the three models. Model Random object What determines its statistics Principal observable Persistent activity, 2012 Increments of a represented coordinate Spike variability, recurrent dynamics, tuning, neural time constants Diffusion of the stored value and readout error Eye drift, 2022 Internal command fluctuations, private motor fluctuations, and measurement noise A circuit model and the downstream filters and feedback Displacement covariance and the eye’s MSD Place fields, 2025 A function of physical position for each cell Spatial covariance, threshold, and spatial dimension Field sizes, counts, shapes, and topology The 2012 and 2022 connection is direct: neural noise can move a maintained eye-position command, which then drives muscles. The 2022 result provides evidence for a substantial shared source before the final motor neurons and shows that integrator diffusion is sufficient within the constructed model. It does not measure the circuit’s Fisher information or test equality in the 2012 bound. The place-field model describes spatially irregular tuning curves. To connect those curves to memory dynamics, we must also specify how the represented position moves. 13.2 How a static map can carry a moving estimate Suppose a network maintains a one-dimensional estimate \(x(t)\) and cell \(i\) has a fixed expected-rate function \(f_i(x)\). Its time-dependent expected rate is \[ R_i(t)=f_i(x(t)). \] Here \(f_i\) describes spatial tuning and \(x(t)\) describes dynamics. A source of time variation has entered even though \(f_i\) is fixed. Actual spike counts add another layer of variability around the expected rate. This construction is a guide calculation connecting the papers’ objects, not a model tested jointly by the three studies. Consider a short interval of duration \(t\) starting at \(x_0\). Assume that the estimate’s local displacement \(\delta x=x(t)-x_0\) has mean zero and variance \(2Dt\), and that it is small enough to linearize each rate curve. Taylor expansion gives \[ f_i(x_0+\delta x) =f_i(x_0)+f_i'(x_0)\delta x+O((\delta x)^2). \] To leading order, the change is \(\delta R_i=f_i'(x_0)\delta x\). Multiplying the centered changes for neurons \(i\) and \(j\) and averaging yields \[ \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_i,\delta R_j) \simeq f_i'(x_0)f_j'(x_0)\operatorname{Var}(\delta x) =2Dt\,f_i'(x_0)f_j'(x_0). \] This covariance concerns expected-rate changes caused by the common represented displacement, conditional on the starting position. It is not a formula for every covariance in a spiking recurrent network. It neglects higher-order changes in tuning and additional private or shared fluctuations. Near a threshold or over a large spatial displacement, the linear approximation must be revisited. 13.2.1 Example: opposite rate changes from the same position error Let the local slopes of two rate curves be \(f_1'=2\) Hz/m and \(f_2'=-1\) Hz/m. Suppose \(D=0.01\) m²/s and the interval is 0.5 s. Then the variance of the common position displacement is \(2Dt=0.01\) m². The contributions to rate variance and covariance are \[ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_1)=2^2(0.01)=0.04\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, \] \[ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_2)=(-1)^2(0.01)=0.01\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_1,\delta R_2)=(2)(-1)(0.01) =-0.02\ \mathrm{Hz}^2. \] With only this one source, the two rate changes have correlation \(-1\): one rises whenever the other falls. Adding independent private noise lowers the magnitude. The negative covariance here comes from opposite tuning slopes under a common position change. It does not establish an inhibitory connection between the cells. For the same slopes, set both expected rates to 10 Hz at the starting position. The upper plot shows the fixed rate curves; the lower plot shows their changes under a common position displacement. Figure 13.1: A common displacement of \(+0.1\) m increases rate 1 by \(0.2\) Hz and decreases rate 2 by \(0.1\) Hz. The changes lie on one line. With displacement variance \(0.01\) m², their covariance is \(-0.02\) Hz² and their correlation is \(-1\). The 10 Hz baseline is chosen only to display positive rates. These are exact lines from the guide’s local example, not recorded data. Both changes are set by the same position displacement, so they occupy one direction in the two-rate plane. Independent private fluctuations would spread them away from that line. Irregular single-cell responses can therefore coexist with population changes along just one direction. To test whether a shared position error causes that pattern, one must measure how the rate changes align with the tuning curves. Field shapes alone do not supply that evidence. 13.3 Each model needs a test matched to its claim The shared-position calculation predicts how rates would change together. Establishing that connection requires measurements of those changes as well as the spatial maps. Each paper tests a different part of the proposed connection: Place-field statistics: A model that matches one distribution may have enough adjustable parameters to do so for several different reasons. The place-field paper gains support by fitting arrangement parameters and then comparing additional features, including slices and shape statistics. The separate firing-rate multiplier used in some comparisons should remain visible when counting how many quantities were predicted without further fitting. A successful high-threshold formula is also a statement about its limiting assumptions; finite-threshold simulations and the original recordings provide different kinds of checks. Eye drift: The eye paper calibrates a movement-to-firing relationship, inverts it, and compares the resulting single-neuron displacement predictions with measured displacement. Shared covariance then carries information that independent private fluctuations cannot supply under the decomposition’s assumptions. The additional MSD comparison tests the time structure: increasing stationary motor-noise amplitude cannot by itself reproduce the accumulating upstream signal. Calibration validity, source correlations, two animals, and horizontal movement remain part of the result’s scope. Memory stability: The 2012 inequality is a mathematical constraint rather than an experimental fit. Its derivation specifies what noise and dynamics it covers. An experimental comparison would need estimates of diffusion, the relevant time constants, and the appropriate instantaneous information rate, all under compatible conditions. Agreement with \(1/N\) scaling alone would not test the entire inequality, since several mechanisms can share that scaling. 13.4 Related studies change assumptions and leave circuit choices open Related studies test the assumptions and ask questions the three papers leave open: Integrating movement: The eye-position account begins with Seung’s line-attractor model. Aksay and colleagues then used recordings and perturbations in goldfish to constrain integrator circuitry. These establish the dynamical problem and experimental architecture behind the 2022 model. Neither supplies the macaque displacement-variance estimate. Burak and Fiete’s earlier grid-cell study examines path integration, updating a position estimate from movement. In its model, velocity drives recurrent population activity, and errors accumulate in the position estimate. Its accuracy ranges belong to the simulated networks and parameter choices, rather than all biological grid circuits.2 Storage capacity and changing synapses: Noise-driven storage also connects to memory capacity. Koyluoglu and colleagues ask how noise limits recall as the delay and number of stored items increase. Their comparison with human data shows why direct storage of several independent values need not capture observed behavior; transformations before and after storage alter the performance prediction. Seeholzer and colleagues examine how short-term changes in synaptic strength affect diffusion and systematic drift. These papers change the storage assumptions rather than invalidate the 2012 calculation inside its original model.3 Recordings from larger environments: For place fields, Eliav and colleagues’ long-tunnel recordings and Harland and colleagues’ large-arena recordings supply the multiple-field, multiple-scale observations. Yartsev and Ulanovsky supply the three-dimensional bat recordings. The 2025 paper reanalyzes those existing data, so its agreement across dimensions is not three newly collected experiments under one protocol. The later study by Maimon and colleagues directly compares CA3 and CA1 in large tunnels: predominantly single fields in CA3 contrast with multiple fields in CA1, while field sizes are similar. That distinction supports treating the CA1 statistics and the upstream spatial circuit as related but separately constrained parts of the explanation.4 Connectivity and learning: Gaussian spatial statistics do not identify a unique pattern of connections. Druckmann and colleagues report structured synaptic connectivity between hippocampal regions. Bittner and colleagues show how electrical events in dendrites, the branching input structures of neurons, can induce changes in synaptic strength and form CA1 place fields. Structure and learning can therefore be present even when a random-function model describes many aggregate field statistics. The model’s success leaves open which circuit mechanism produces these maps. Input, connectivity, learning, or perturbation measurements could distinguish the possibilities.5 Benefits for perception: The source and use of eye motion are different questions. Nghiem and colleagues combine human eye tracking with a model of how eye movement affects visual signals to explain why an intermediate amount of fixational motion can help fine visual discrimination. A movement that partly originates from internal noise can still have useful sensory consequences, and feedback can regulate its statistics. Benefit for perception does not uniquely identify the neural generator.6 13.5 A joint test would compare tuning maps with population fluctuations A joint test needs tuning maps and fluctuations from the same population. A possible sequence is: Estimate the tuning maps and their uncertainty. Measure fluctuations when external signals provide little correction of the represented position. Test whether their covariance aligns with the changes implied by the tuning maps. Fit diffusion only over a range where the local approximation and measurement corrections are justified. If comparing behavior, include the physical or neural filters between the representation and the measurement. This would ask whether one system satisfies both spatial-statistics and dynamical-stability constraints. A static Gaussian-process fit alone cannot supply the diffusion coefficient. A diffusion fit alone cannot establish the distribution of fields. A joint success would be more restrictive, while a mismatch would point to a particular assumption to change: spatial input statistics, recurrent maintenance, the observation filter, or their coupling.
